/guides/visual-reaction-time.title: Human Visual Reaction Time: Physiology, Measurement & Real-World Latency
/guides/visual-reaction-time.subtitle: An in-depth review of sensory phototransduction, neural transmission delays, and browser-based benchmarking boundaries.

sections.heading: The Physiological Visual Reflex Arc
paragraphs: Human reaction time to a visual cue is governed by a cascade of discrete physiological stages. First, retinal phototransduction converts incident light into electrical impulses within approximately 20 to 40 milliseconds.
Second, the signal travels along the optic nerve through the lateral geniculate nucleus to the primary visual cortex (V1), consuming an additional 20 to 30 milliseconds.
Third, central processing, motor cortex activation, and efferent nerve propagation to muscle fibers in the finger require roughly 80 to 100 milliseconds.

Combined, the absolute physiological threshold for human simple visual response latency sits near 150 milliseconds under ideal laboratory conditions, with typical healthy adult responses averaging between 200 and 260 milliseconds.

sections.heading: Browser vs Laboratory Benchmarking
paragraphs: Browser-based measurements cannot directly isolate biological neural conduction. Hardware polling intervals, wireless input latency, operating system task scheduling, and monitor refresh intervals introduce systematic variance.
On a standard 60 Hz display, visual stimulus presentation can be delayed by up to 16.7 milliseconds depending on where in the refresh cycle the update lands.
PULSE captures raw high-resolution performance timestamps at the browser event boundary without subtracting theoretical offsets. This ensures transparent, reproducible benchmarking across devices.
listItems: Display refresh quantization introduces 0 to 16.7ms of variance on 60Hz panels.
Standard USB mouse polling rates (125Hz to 1000Hz) add 1 to 8ms of input jitter.
PULSE flags anticipatory responses below 80.0ms as false starts to maintain benchmark validity.

sections.heading: Biological and Environmental Modulators
paragraphs: Reaction latency is not a fixed physiological constant. Circadian rhythms, sleep debt, cognitive fatigue, and caffeine intake cause significant day-to-day fluctuations.
Longitudinal personal benchmarking provides greater insight than single-session comparisons, revealing patterns in baseline cognitive readiness.

/guides/stroop-effect-speed.title: The Stroop Effect: Cognitive Interference, Speed of Processing & Inhibition
/guides/stroop-effect-speed.subtitle: Understanding cognitive control, automated word reading, and how response latency reflects mental conflict resolution.

sections.heading: The Mechanism of Cognitive Conflict
paragraphs: First described by John Ridley Stroop in 1935, the Stroop effect illustrates the interference between automated cognitive routines and intentional task demands.
When naming the font color of an incongruent word (e.g., the word 'RED' printed in blue ink), reaction times are systematically slower compared to congruent stimuli.
This difference, termed conflict cost or interference latency, reflects the executive time required by the anterior cingulate cortex and prefrontal regions to suppress automatic reading.

sections.heading: Deriving Conflict and Interference Costs
paragraphs: In modern cognitive benchmarking, two distinct metrics are derived: congruent response latency and incongruent response latency.
The net difference represents interference cost. Lower conflict costs indicate superior selective attention and inhibitory control.
PULSE records individual trial latencies and rejects anticipatory inputs under 80.01 milliseconds to ensure genuine decision-making measurements.

/benchmarks/cognitive-percentiles.title: PULSE Cognitive Benchmarks: Session-Level Empirical Distributions
/benchmarks/cognitive-percentiles.subtitle: Scientific methodology, sample thresholds, and preliminary reference distributions for browser-based reaction latency.

sections.heading: Session-Level Empirical Distribution Contract
paragraphs: PULSE reports session-level empirical distributions rather than claiming universal biological population norms.

Because browser tests are conducted without laboratory calibration or participant credential verification, single users may complete multiple sessions. Benchmarks describe verified session observations under real-world device conditions.
Distributions are strictly segregated by assessment protocol, metric derivation, and device input class (desktop keyboard vs touchscreen).

sections.heading: Statistical Publication Criteria
paragraphs: To avoid misleading users with premature statistics, PULSE enforces strict publication gates. Benchmark tables remain in a verified dataPending state until cohorts meet our precision requirements.
Median (P50) and quartile (P25, P75) publication requires a minimum of 500 completed sessions per demographic group with bootstrap standard error under 2.5% of the median.
Extreme tail quantiles (P99) are unavailable in the initial release due to monitor refresh quantization and operating system task interruption variances.

sections.heading: External Laboratory Reference Norms
paragraphs: While PULSE session data gathers to satisfy the statistical threshold, the following external peer-reviewed laboratory baselines provide general reference points.

In Woods et al. (2015), healthy adult visual reaction time under calibrated lab timers averaged 231 milliseconds (IQR: 215ms - 258ms). Browser-measured latency is typically 20ms to 40ms higher due to hardware polling intervals.
